title: What a fund is: pool, AMC, scheme, units, NAV, AUM
objectives: Explain a mutual fund as a pool of money run by an AMC, in plain words.
Say what a unit and a NAV are, and work out units from an amount and a NAV.
body_md:
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it as one portfolio, managed by a professional fund manager and regulated by SEBI. The company that runs the schemes is the AMC (Asset Management Company). Each scheme is one specific fund with its own objective.

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mutual fund | A pool of money from many investors, managed by a professional fund manager and regulated by SEBI | 10 lakh investors each put in small amounts; the fund buys 60 stocks for all of them |
| AMC (Asset Management Company) | The company that runs the mutual fund schemes | The AMC appoints the fund manager and publishes the NAV |
| Scheme | One specific fund with its own objective, e.g. a large-cap fund | One AMC can run 40+ schemes |
| Unit | Your share of the fund. You buy units, not shares | ₹10,000 at NAV ₹50 = 200 units |
| NAV (Net Asset Value) | Price of one unit = (value of the fund's holdings − expenses) ÷ units. Declared once every business day | Fund worth ₹500 crore with 10 crore units → NAV ₹50 |
| AUM (Assets Under Management) | Total money a fund or AMC manages | "This fund has ₹12,000 crore AUM" |

> **Talk-track:** “Think of a mutual fund as a shared basket. Your money buys units in it. The NAV is today's price of one unit; it moves because the things in the basket move.”

> **Investor takeaway:** A low NAV does not mean a fund is cheap, and a high NAV does not mean it is expensive. What matters is how the NAV grows.
example: ₹10,000 invested at a NAV of ₹50 buys 200 units. If the NAV rises to ₹55, those units are worth ₹11,000.
